The Payton Family Tree

The Payton family tree follows the Payton, Hancock, Duncan, Jourdan, Buchanan, Thorp, and Jolly lines across nine generations — from Scotland and Revolutionary-era Virginia through Kentucky, Alabama, Tennessee, and Georgia to Texas, and on to the family’s homes today in Arizona, New Mexico, Iowa, and California. Every person in the tree has a dossier below, and where records disagree, both readings are shown as a conflict rather than quietly harmonized.

How sure are we? Documented Tree-sourced Family account Lead Conflict Unproven but not contradicted Unknown A record or authoritative source; a compiled tree only; something the family itself reports; a single weak source; two sources that disagree (both shown); a claim carried on a stated basis, with no record against it; or not yet found.

Full tree shows everyone in the tree — direct ancestors plus siblings, cousins, and branch families, each labeled with how well they are documented. Switch to Direct lineage to see only the direct ancestor lines.

Migration — the bloodlines across America

The same lines, drawn as movement instead of descent. Each path steps through where successive generations of that bloodline were born, lived, and died. These lines run through the South — Virginia, the Carolinas, Georgia, Tennessee, and Alabama into Texas — and funnel into Austin, Texas: nearly every one of them passes through it. Transatlantic origins sit at the map’s edge as tags with an arrow to the first American waypoint; Europe itself isn’t plotted. Every dot is a place tied to people in the tree. Austin is the hub: the living generations branch out from it to Surprise, Albuquerque, Polk City, and Palo Alto. Lines that rest on DAR lineage, sourced trees, or family notes carry the same status labels as the chart. Press Play the movement to watch the lines arrive in chronological order. Schematic — city-level, not to scale.

Ask the tree

Questions a visitor might ask, answered in advance from the dossiers on this page — there is no live AI here and nothing is made up at the moment you ask. Each answer is written from the same records as the profiles, carries the same evidence label (Documented, Tree-sourced, Family account, Unproven but not contradicted, Conflict), and says plainly when something is not known yet. Type a name or a few words from your question, browse by topic, or tap any question to open its answer — most answers end with a button that jumps to the full dossier.

Sources & how this tree was built

Every claim on this page carries the strength of the source behind it — that is what the confidence labels mean. This section names the record sets used and how disagreements are handled, so any entry can be checked or re-done by someone else.

Method, in order
  • Generation by generation, record by record. A parent was only added when a record named them — a marriage record naming both sets of parents, a death record naming parents — never by surname matching alone.
  • Image before index. Where a register or census page could be opened, the entry was read off the image and called image-verified. Index-only hits are labelled as such in the dossier.
  • Conflicts are kept, not harmonised. When two records disagree (a birth year, a surname, a birthplace), both readings stay in the dossier and in the Conflicts section, with the current adjudication.
  • Family accounts stay labelled. What the family itself reports is labelled Family account and kept separate from documented fact — it is never silently promoted to fact.
The record sets
  • The Payton lines: the DAR ancestor and descendants database (George Duncan, #A034872), Fluvanna County will and probate (1783), Jackson County, Alabama estate records, Swofford’s Our Bachman Ancestors and Our Kin (1979), the Jourdan-Bachman Pioneer Farms Foundation, Monsanto internal Technical Services reports 1967–68 (Washington University Monsanto Company Records), U.S. censuses, Texas death certificates, and the SSDI.
  • Compiled trees and family accounts sit at the bottom of the hierarchy: they supply leads and names to test, and an entry that rests on one says so.

Everyone in the tree — dossiers

Each dossier is organised the same way: a facts table (dates, occupation, places, family, evidence strength), then what the records say, then a historical context box — the world around that person, clearly marked as general background rather than a record about them — and a sources & method note. A card for every person in the dataset through November 1, 2026: birth, marriages, death and burial, children, siblings, occupations, residences, and military service where records give them. Use search to find a name, then tap Show in the tree on their card to jump straight to them in the chart above — that is the quickest way to reach the earliest generations, such as Thomas Payton of Bisley at the top of the Peyton line. In Direct lineage view, branch-only people (siblings, cousins, in-laws) are hidden; in Full tree view, everyone appears. The dossiers are ordered oldest to youngest by birth — Thomas Payton of Bisley comes first, and the living generations come last.

How to read this tree

Every fact in the dossiers below carries one of these labels. They say how well a fact is backed — not whether it is likely or interesting.

Documented
Backed by an actual record that was read firsthand: a census page, a birth/marriage/death certificate, a will, a church register entry, or a comparable primary source.
Tree-sourced
Taken from someone's online family tree (such as the FamilySearch tree) with no underlying record found behind it yet. A lead, not evidence — it may be right, but it has not been verified.
Family account
Told by a family member (for example, something a family member recalls about their own parents). Kept and labeled as family testimony, separate from records.
Conflict Unproven but not contradicted
Two real records disagree about the same fact (a date, a place, a spelling). Both versions are shown; neither is silently picked.
Contested
The weight of the evidence leans one way, but a credible source says otherwise. Adjudicated as best the records allow, but not proven.
Unproven but not contradicted
A claim carried in the tree because nothing in the records contradicts it — but not yet proven either. The card always states its basis in words, and the basis differs by kind: DAR lineage / sourced trees (underlying records not yet checked), a named family note (the Buchanan notebook, the Moore family record, the Barnes Bible), or a spoken family account. Sourced is not the same as proven, and lore is not lumped in with either.
Not found
Searched for in the relevant records and not found. That does not prove the record never existed — coverage has gaps, and the dossier says what was searched.

Conflicts, kept as conflicts

These disagreements are part of the record. Both readings are shown, with the current adjudication — nothing below has been silently harmonized.

Compiled from the family’s genealogy research through November 1, 2026. Sources are named with each entry — among them the DAR ancestor and descendants database, Fluvanna County will and probate records, U.S. censuses, the Social Security Death Index, Texas death certificates, Monsanto internal reports (1967–68), the Jourdan-Bachman Pioneer Farms Foundation, and compiled family trees. Where a value rests on a single tree or a family account, the entry says so. No invented illustrations are used: a portrait appears only where a real photograph attributable to that person has been sourced, with its provenance stated. No addresses or contact details for living people are published.
